To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the microbiota composition of saliva is associated with lung function and that this association is not explained by HIV infection.
Salivary microbiota signatures are associated with pulmonary function and lung disease in HIV infected patients.

HIV infection and cigarette smoking, but not HIV treatment with ART, are associated with a distinct salivary bacterial community structure, and that these differences in salivary microbial composition correlate with airway dysfunction.

the question of how a person can be healthy in the face of the many challenges to health.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the oral cavity and the lung are two different organs with different microbial communities.
the gut microbiome is not associated with the presence or progression of COPD.
the oral and intestinal microbiota are altered in HIV-infected patients and that these alterations are associated with pulmonary dysfunction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is not the number of bacteria that matters, but the type of bacterial species that are present.
we found a dysbiotic oral microbial signature that was associated with pulmonary dysfunction and inflammation in HIV infected subjects.
we are in a new era of precision medicine in pulmonary hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HIV infection and ART exposure can have profound effects on the composition of the lung microbiota, with the potential to alter the host immune response and influence the risk of lung disease in this population.
the oral cavity may be a useful site to sample the microbiome to predict the development and severity of pulmonary disease.
we should be aware that oral microbiota dysbiosis can occur in HIV infected subjects with lung inflammation, and that this is not necessarily related to active smoking.
